To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

in a rural Amazonian setting, children had more adequate diets than their mothers and that this maternal-child dietary buffering was related to child age, child height-for-age, maternal lactation status, and household food availability.

in a context of food scarcity in a low-resource setting, children have more adequate energy and protein diets than their mothers, and that this is due to the combined effect of the child's age and height-for age, the mother's reproductive status, and household food availability.

(1) in a context of food scarcity and undernutrition, children have more adequate energy and protein intakes than their mother; (2) maternal-child energy and/or protein inequalities are negatively associated with child age and height for age and positively associated with lactation; (3) maternal-child energy inequalities are positively associated with household food availability; and (4) maternal-child protein inequalities are negatively related to household food availability
In summary, our research is concerned with
the extent to which maternal-child dietary inequalities are a function of food scarcity in a rural Amazonian community.
the following question: how do mothers and their children cope in a setting of resource scarcity and how does this coping strategy affect the nutritional status of children?
how maternal-child dietary inequalities are shaped by the household context and maternal and child characteristics in a setting of resource scarcity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the maternal-child buffering effect exists in this rural Amazonian setting but that it is not absolute.

in this context of food insecurity, children's dietary energy and protein adequacies are higher than those of their mothers and that the degree of these maternal-child inequalities is influenced by household-level food availability, child age and gender and maternal reproductive status.

in this context of food insecurity, the majority of children in this rural Amazonian setting had adequate intakes of energy and protein, while the majority of their mothers were in a negative energy balance and had inadequate protein intakes, suggesting the presence of maternal-child buffering.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the maternal buffering hypothesis holds in the Amazonian context, but only under conditions of food abundance.
the buffering hypothesis holds true in a setting of extreme food scarcity.

maternal-child dietary inequalities were present in this setting of food scarcity, but that the extent of these inequalities was influenced by the degree of food scarcity in the household and individual child factors such as age, height-for-age and gender.
The main takeaway from our work is that
mothers and children are not always equally vulnerable to food scarcity and that children's diets can be more adequate than their mothers' diets under certain conditions.
the mother-child relationship is a key factor in understanding the dietary inequalities of mother-child dyads in the rural Amazon.
the mother-child pair should be considered the unit of analysis for nutritional assessments in settings of food scarcity.
